COMPULSORY ELECTIVE AREA

COMPULSORY ELECTIVE AREA 1 · JUNE

The bicycle

A bicycle is full of mathematics. The tyre shows its size in inches and in millimetres, the chainring has more teeth than the sprocket, and changing gear changes a gear ratio. You work out how far a wheel rolls in one turn, which frame height suits you and how fast you ride in which gear. At the end you present your own bikes.

8 LESSONS2 UNITSPROJECT
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • convert tyre sizes between inches and millimetres and read the marking 37-622
  • work out the wheel circumference and the distance per turn of the wheel, find the right frame height
  • find the gear ratio from the chainring and the sprocket
  • work out the distance per crank turn and the speed from the cadence and present your results

$3 : 1$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Tyre size and wheel circumference

A tyre says “37-622” and “28 x 1 3/8 x 1 5/8”. The first marking is the exact one: the tyre is 37 mm wide and fits a rim with a diameter of 622 mm. The second is an old marking in inches, and the “28 inches” is more of a name than a measurement.

KEY POINT · TYRE SIZE AND WHEEL CIRCUMFERENCE

$1\,\text{inch} = 2.54\,\text{cm} = 25.4\,\text{mm}$

The marking 37-622 means: tyre width 37 mm, rim diameter 622 mm. The wheel diameter is about $622\,\text{mm} + 2 \cdot 37\,\text{mm} = 696\,\text{mm}$.

The wheel circumference $u = \pi \cdot d$ is the distance the wheel covers in one turn. For a distance $s$ it needs $s : u$ turns.

Frame height (rule of thumb for trekking bikes): inside leg length · 0.66.

A name, not a measurement: a 28-inch wheel usually has a diameter of just under 70 cm, not exactly $28 \cdot 2.54\,\text{cm} = 71.12\,\text{cm}$.

Bike computers need the wheel circumference in millimetres, otherwise they show a wrong speed.

INTERACTIVE · WHAT DOES THE TYRE SAY?

Choose a wheel size and change the tyre width. The wheel diameter is the rim plus twice the tyre.

EXAMPLE 1 · THE TYRE 37-622

Work out the wheel diameter, the wheel circumference and the number of turns of the wheel for 1 km.

$d \approx 622 + 2 \cdot 37 = 696\,\text{mm}$, $\;u = \pi \cdot 696\,\text{mm} \approx 2187\,\text{mm} \approx 2.19\,\text{m}$.

$1000\,\text{m} : 2.187\,\text{m} \approx 457$

About 2.19 m per turn, roughly 457 turns per kilometre.

EXAMPLE 2 · CONVERTING INCHES

How many centimetres are 26 inches? How many inches are 700 mm?

$26 \cdot 2.54\,\text{cm} = 66.04\,\text{cm}$. $\;700\,\text{mm} : 25.4\,\text{mm} \approx 27.6$.

26 inches are 66.04 cm, 700 mm are about 27.6 inches.

EXERCISES

Convert into centimetres: 20 inches, 24 inches, 29 inches.

50.8 cm, 60.96 cm, 73.66 cm

Work out the wheel diameter and the wheel circumference. a) 47-406   b) 54-559

a) $406 + 94 = 500\,\text{mm}$, $u \approx 1571\,\text{mm} \approx 1.57\,\text{m}$   b) $559 + 108 = 667\,\text{mm}$, $u \approx 2095\,\text{mm} \approx 2.10\,\text{m}$

A wheel has a circumference of 2.10 m. How many turns does it make on a way to school 15 km long?

$15{,}000 : 2.1 \approx 7143$ turns.

Use the rule of thumb to work out the right frame height for an inside leg length of 78 cm and of 85 cm.

$78 \cdot 0.66 \approx 51.5\,\text{cm}$ and $85 \cdot 0.66 \approx 56.1\,\text{cm}$

In a bike computer the wheel circumference is set to 2000 mm; in reality it is 2187 mm. The computer shows $20\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$. How fast are you really going? Does it show too much or too little?

The computer counts turns and calculates with too little distance per turn: $20 \cdot \tfrac{2187}{2000} \approx 21.9\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$. It shows too little.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many centimetres are 28 inches?

$28 \cdot 2.54 = 71.12$

$622 + 80 = 702\,\text{mm}$

A wheel has a diameter of 700 mm. How many metres does it roll in one turn? Round to two decimal places.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Gear ratio and speed

The chainring has 44 teeth, the sprocket 11. In one turn of the crank the chain pulls 44 links over the sprocket. For that the sprocket has to turn four times, and the rear wheel with it. So one turn of the crank gives four turns of the wheel.

KEY POINT · GEAR RATIO AND SPEED

Gear ratio $i = \dfrac{\text{teeth on the chainring}}{\text{teeth on the sprocket}}$. In one turn of the crank the rear wheel turns $i$ times.

Distance per crank turn = $i \cdot u$.

Speed = cadence · distance per crank turn. With the cadence in turns per minute and the distance in metres, this gives metres per minute. Times 60 and divided by 1000 gives $\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$.

Large $i$: high gear, fast. Small $i$: low gear, good on hills.

Converting: $1\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{min}} = 0.06\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$.

Comfortable cadences are between 60 and 90 turns per minute. Anyone who wants to go faster changes gear instead of pedalling faster.

INTERACTIVE · THE GEARS

Choose the tyre size, change the chainring, the sprocket and the cadence. The table works out the speed.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE GEAR 44/16

A bike with a circumference of 2.19 m rides in the gear 44/16 with 70 crank turns per minute. How fast is it?

$i = \tfrac{44}{16} = 2.75$. Distance per crank turn: $2.75 \cdot 2.19\,\text{m} \approx 6.02\,\text{m}$. Per minute: $70 \cdot 6.02\,\text{m} \approx 421\,\text{m}$.

$421 \cdot 60\,\text{m} \approx 25.3\,\text{km}$ per hour.

EXAMPLE 4 · WHICH SPROCKET?

Someone wants to ride at $20\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$ with 60 crank turns per minute. The wheel has a circumference of 2.2 m, the chainring 38 teeth. Which sprocket fits?

$20\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} = 20{,}000\,\text{m} : 60 \approx 333\,\text{m}$ per minute, so $333 : 60 \approx 5.56\,\text{m}$ per crank turn. $i = 5.56 : 2.2 \approx 2.53$.

Sprocket: $38 : 2.53 \approx 15$ teeth.

EXERCISES

Work out the gear ratio. a) 48/12   b) 36/18   c) 32/24   d) 28/32

a) 4   b) 2   c) $\approx 1.33$   d) 0.875 (less than 1: a climbing gear)

A wheel has a circumference of 2.1 m, the gear ratio is 3. How far do you go with one turn of the crank?

$3 \cdot 2.1\,\text{m} = 6.3\,\text{m}$

With 80 crank turns per minute you get 5 m per turn. How fast are you in $\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$?

$80 \cdot 5\,\text{m} = 400\,\text{m}$ per minute, $400 \cdot 60 = 24{,}000\,\text{m}$ per hour: $24\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$.

You get 6.3 m per crank turn. How many crank turns do you need for 10 km? How long does that take at 70 turns per minute?

$10{,}000 : 6.3 \approx 1587$ turns, $1587 : 70 \approx 22.7$ minutes.

A mountain bike has three chainrings at the front (22, 32 and 44 teeth) and nine sprockets at the back from 11 to 34 teeth. Work out the smallest and the largest gear ratio. How many gears are there in theory? Why are not all of them useful?

Smallest: $\tfrac{22}{34} \approx 0.65$, largest: $\tfrac{44}{11} = 4$. In theory $3 \cdot 9 = 27$ gears. Some give almost the same ratio, and with a large chainring and a large sprocket the chain runs at a very steep angle.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is the gear ratio of the gear 42/14?

$\tfrac{42}{14} = 3$

$i = 2.5$ and $u = 2\,\text{m}$. How far do you go with one turn of the crank?

$2.5 \cdot 2\,\text{m} = 5\,\text{m}$

60 crank turns per minute and 5 m per turn: how many $\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$ is that?

300 m per minute, 18,000 m per hour: $18\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A cyclist rides at 6 metres per second. How many kilometres per hour is that?

$6 \cdot 3.6 = 21.6\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$

Connect with chapter 2.1: at a steady cadence of 70 turns per minute, the speed $v$ (in $\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$) is proportional to the distance $e$ per crank turn (in m). Give the equation.

$v = 70 \cdot e \cdot 60 : 1000 = 4.2 \cdot e$. With 6 m per turn: $25.2\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$.

Connect with chapter 3.1: how many times as often does a 20-inch wheel turn as a 28-inch wheel over the same distance? Calculate with the sizes in inches.

The circumferences are in the same ratio as the diameters: $\tfrac{28}{20} = 1.4$. The small wheel turns 1.4 times as often.

Project: a profile of your bike. In groups, examine a bicycle: tyre marking, diameter, circumference, all the chainrings and sprockets, smallest and largest gear ratio, speed at 70 crank turns per minute in the lowest and in the highest gear. Design a poster and present it.

Individual. Check each other’s calculations and compare your bikes: which one has the advantage on hills, which one on a flat stretch?

EXCURSIONHISTORY

From the running machine to the chain-driven bike

On 12 June 1817, Karl Drais rode his running machine from Mannheim to the Schwetzingen coaching inn and back, about 14 km in just under an hour. His wooden bike weighed about 22 kg and had no pedals: you pushed yourself along with your feet. That gives an average of about $15\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$.

Around 1870 the penny-farthings came. Their pedals sat directly on the front wheel, so one turn of the crank was one turn of the wheel, as with the gear ratio $i = 1$. Anyone who wanted to ride fast therefore needed a huge front wheel, sometimes 1.5 m high. Only the chain made gear ratios possible: with small wheels of the same size and a big chainring you get just as far per pedal stroke, but much more safely.

Sources: City of Mannheim, leaflet “Karl Drais – 200 Jahre Fahrrad” (2017). Technoseum Mannheim, exhibition on the history of the bicycle.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

TYRE SIZE

1 inch = 2.54 cm; 37-622: diameter ≈ 622 + 2 · 37 = 696 mm

26 inches = 66.04 cm

WHEEL CIRCUMFERENCE

$u = \pi \cdot d$, turns = distance : circumference

$d = 696\,\text{mm}$: $u \approx 2.19\,\text{m}$

GEAR RATIO

$i$ = teeth at the front : teeth at the back; distance per crank turn $i \cdot u$

44/16: $i = 2.75$

SPEED

cadence · distance per crank turn, in m/min, times 0.06 gives km/h

$70 \cdot 6.02\,\text{m} \approx 421\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{min}} \approx 25.3\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$

$\tfrac{52}{13} = 4$

ROUND 2 · WITH A CALCULATOR

How big is the wheel circumference with the marking 54-559? Round to two decimal places in metres.

$d = 667\,\text{mm}$, $u = \pi \cdot 0.667\,\text{m} \approx 2.10\,\text{m}$

How many turns does a wheel with a circumference of 2.10 m make over 1 km? Round to whole turns.

$1000 : 2.1 \approx 476$

Gear 40/16, wheel circumference 2.16 m, 70 crank turns per minute: how fast do you go? Round to one decimal place.

$i = 2.5$, $2.5 \cdot 2.16 = 5.4\,\text{m}$, $70 \cdot 5.4 = 378\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{min}}$, times 0.06: $22.68 \approx 22.7\,\tfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}}$
